Two refinements matter in interviews. First, push_back is O(1) amortized, not worst case: a dynamic array doubles its capacity when full, so one push occasionally costs O(n) to copy everything, but n pushes cost at most about 2n element copies in total, which averages to O(1) each. Second, the O(log n) search only works on sorted data; sorting first costs O(n log n), so it pays off only if you search many times.

Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because every later element shifts one slot. Edge cases: index -1 or n is out of bounds (Python silently wraps -1, which hides bugs), and an empty array has no valid index. Linked lists invert these costs: O(1) insert given a node, O(n) access.

Average O(1) rests on two assumptions: the hash function spreads keys roughly uniformly over m buckets, and the load factor (entries divided by buckets) stays bounded because the table resizes, typically doubling past about 0.75. Then each chain has constant expected length. Resizing costs O(n) but is amortized away exactly like a dynamic array.

The worst case is O(n) when many keys collide, by accident with a poor hash or on purpose through hash-flooding inputs; Java 8 converts long chains into balanced trees (O(log n)) and Python randomizes string hashes per process. Keys must be hashable and effectively immutable: a Python list cannot be a key, a tuple can. Do not rely on iteration order for unordered_map or HashSet.

Brute force checks all n(n-1)/2 pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Sorting then using two pointers is O(n log n) but destroys the original indices unless you sort (value, index) pairs. The hash map gives O(n) time at O(n) space, with no assumption that the input is sorted, positive, or free of duplicates; negatives and zero work unchanged.

The same element may not be used twice: for nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 the answer is [1, 2], not [0, 0]. Duplicates are fine: [3, 3] with target 6 gives [0, 1]. In fixed-width integers, target - x can overflow when values sit near the type limits, so widen to 64 bits. Siblings: Two Sum II (sorted), 3Sum, 4Sum, counting pairs, Two Sum on a BST.

Correctness invariant: before processing index i, the map holds every value from nums[0..i-1]. If a valid pair (j, i) with j < i exists, then nums[j] is in the map when we reach i, so the lookup finds it; and the first i that completes a pair is exactly when we return. Every pair is considered once, from the later index.

Checking before inserting is what prevents pairing an element with itself and what makes [3, 3] work: at i = 1 we need 3, find it at index 0, and return [0, 1]. If duplicates overwrite an earlier index, nothing breaks, because any stored index still holds the right value. Time is O(n) expected; space is O(n) in the worst case, e.g. when no pair exists and all values get stored.

Classic bugs. Inserting before checking lets [3] with target 6 return [0, 0]. In a two-pass version (build the whole map, then query) you must verify map[need] != i, otherwise an element matches itself, and with duplicates the stored index may be the later one. In Python, naming the dict map shadows the built-in, so prefer seen. Returning [-1, -1] is a contract choice; many judges guarantee exactly one solution, but ask.

If the task is to count pairs rather than find one, store frequencies and add freq[need] before incrementing freq[x]. Variant for system-design flavored interviews: design a Two Sum data structure with add(x) and find(sum), where you choose whether to optimize add (O(1), find O(n) scanning the map) or find.

In Python, create the seen-set with set(), since {} is an empty dict with no add. Duplicate detection is O(n) time and O(n) space; the alternative is sort then compare neighbors, O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space if you may mutate the input. Counting is also available as collections.Counter.

For anagrams with lowercase letters, a 26-slot integer array replaces the dict: O(1) space and a smaller constant. For Unicode, keep a map. The equal-length check up front is essential, since the decrement pass cannot detect surplus letters in a longer t unless you also stop when a count goes negative. Extensions: Group Anagrams (key = sorted string or a 26-count tuple), Top K Frequent (bucket by frequency, O(n)), Longest Consecutive Sequence (set; start counting only at x where x-1 is absent).

Duplicates policy matters. Two Sum can overwrite, but 'first index of each value' needs setdefault or a check before assigning, and counting pairs needs frequencies. Never mutate a collection while iterating it: Python raises RuntimeError, Java throws ConcurrentModificationException. Beware defaultdict: merely reading freq[k] inserts the key with 0, which inflates len(freq) and breaks any check that assumes every key has a positive count.

Memory is real: a Python dict entry with boxed ints costs on the order of 100 bytes, so 10 million entries can exceed a gigabyte; sorting plus two pointers may then be the better trade. Avoid floating-point keys because equality is fragile. In C++ with adversarial tests, std::unordered_map with its default hash can be attacked; a randomized custom hash fixes that.

Recognition checklist. 'Have I seen this before?' means a set. 'What was associated with this key?' means a map. 'How many of each?' means a frequency map. 'Is there an earlier element that completes a condition with the current one?' means a one-pass map of complements. The one-pass idea extends to any condition expressible as a function of the current element, such as x - k or x XOR y.

Choose the structure by key space: if keys are small integers or letters, a plain array beats a hash table in speed and memory. If memory is tight or the data is already sorted, two pointers uses O(1) space. If you need ordering queries (nearest larger key), use a balanced tree or sorted structure instead, at O(log n) per operation.
leetcode-arrays-01.further: Reach for hashing when the brute force is a nested loop whose inner loop only asks 'does a particular value exist?' or 'how many times?'. Close siblings: two pointers (needs sorted order, O(1) space), prefix sums plus a map (turns subarray-sum questions into complement lookups), and sliding window (also uses a map, but only over the current window). Sorting is the alternative when you need order rather than membership. To tell them apart, ask whether elements must be contiguous, whether input is sorted, and whether memory is limited. Follow-ups: Contains Duplicate, Valid Anagram, Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements, Longest Consecutive Sequence, 3Sum, Subarray Sum Equals K.

The invariant is what turns a heuristic into a proof. For the palindrome: before every iteration, each mirrored pair (k, n-1-k) with k < l has been verified equal, ignoring junk characters. The loop ends when l >= r, leaving at most one unchecked character, and a single character always matches itself, so the whole string is a palindrome. A mismatch is a concrete witness, so returning false immediately is correct.

Each iteration moves at least one pointer toward the other and never backward, so the work is at most n steps: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Building the cleaned string and comparing it with its reverse is also O(n) time but costs O(n) space. An empty string, or one containing only punctuation, is a palindrome vacuously.

The cleaned string amanaplanacanalpanama has 21 characters, an odd count, so the middle character c is compared only with itself and the pointers meet there. Even lengths end with l just past r. Test both parities.

Definition details to confirm in an interview: digits count as alphanumeric, so '0P' is not a palindrome (0 differs from p), and case folding applies only to letters. For non-ASCII text, isalnum and lowercasing depend on the locale or Unicode rules; ask whether to handle it.

A natural follow-up is Valid Palindrome II (may delete at most one character): at the first mismatch, test whether skipping either s[l] or s[r] leaves a palindrome. That is still O(n), since each branch is a linear check. Counting palindromic substrings instead uses expand-around-center in O(n^2).

Both skip loops need the guard l < r. Without it, an all-punctuation string such as '...' lets r run below l, and in Python s[-1] silently wraps around, hiding the bug instead of crashing. With the guard the pointers can meet but never cross during skipping.

Every pointer move is justified: skipped characters are defined as irrelevant, so ignoring them cannot hide a mismatch. A common worry is that the nested while loops make this O(n^2). They do not: the pointers never move backward, so all inner iterations together advance l and r at most n times in total; this is amortized analysis.

Portability: in C or C++, isalnum on a negative char value is undefined behavior, so cast to unsigned char; or test ranges directly ('a' to 'z', '0' to '9' after lowercasing).

Trace the tricky input 'a.': l = 0, r = 1. The l-skip does nothing; the r-skip sees '.', so r becomes 0. Now l == r, and the comparison checks 'a' against itself, which passes. Then l = 1 and r = -1, the outer condition fails, and the result is true. This works only because of the l < r guards inside the skip loops.

Other checks: empty string gives r = -1, loop never runs, true. A single character, true. Time O(n), space O(1); a recursive version would use O(n) stack. Language shortcuts such as Python's s[l].isalnum() and s[l].lower() are Unicode aware, while hand-rolled ASCII checks are not. The compare-then-move order matters: moving before comparing would skip pairs, which is the off-by-one the pitfalls panel warns about.

A clarification: the sorted pair-sum moves the pointers toward each other (opposite directions). The same-direction family (reader and writer) appears in the next panel's duplicate removal.

Proof of safety: if a[i] + a[j] > target and the array is sorted, then for every i' >= i the sum a[i'] + a[j] >= a[i] + a[j] > target, so j cannot pair with anything still in play; earlier indices were already eliminated. Discarding j loses no solution. The < case is symmetric for i. Each step discards one index, so at most n-1 steps: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Trace [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15], target 15: 1+15=16 (j--), 1+11=12 (i++), 2+11=13 (i++), 4+11=15 found at indices 2 and 4.

Pair sum on [2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 15] with target 10: 2+15=17 so j--; 2+11=13 so j--; 2+8=10, found. Container With Most Water: moving the shorter line is safe because any container that keeps the shorter line but has a smaller width has height at most that line and less width, so its area cannot beat the current one; thus the shorter line is useless for the rest of the search. On ties, either side works. O(n) overall.

Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array: start w = 1, and copy a[r] to a[w] only when a[r] != a[w-1], then return w; the empty array is a special case. Relatives: 3Sum (sort, fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates, O(n^2)), Trapping Rain Water, Sort Colors (three pointers), Move Zeroes, Squares of a Sorted Array.

Use l < r for pair problems: with l <= r the same element could be used twice, which Two Sum II forbids. For palindromes either works, but l < r is cleaner. Always test lengths 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 to cover both parities.

Sorted input is the usual prerequisite. For Two Sum with original indices on unsorted data, sorting destroys the positions unless you carry them along, so a hash map is simpler.

In 3Sum, duplicates produce repeated triples unless you skip equal values after a hit on both pointers and also skip equal outer values. Sums can overflow 32-bit ints, so widen. The deepest pitfall is moving a pointer without a proof: always write down why the discarded element cannot belong to any remaining solution, as with the shorter wall in Container With Most Water.
leetcode-arrays-02.further: Reach for two pointers when the input is sorted, when you compare or pair elements from both ends (palindromes, pair sums), or when you partition or compact an array in place with O(1) space. Closest siblings: sliding window (both pointers move forward and the interval between them carries running state), binary search (halves the range using a midpoint, O(log n) rather than linear), and hashing (handles unsorted input at O(n) space). Test: can you argue that one pointer can be discarded forever? Follow-ups: Two Sum II, 3Sum, 3Sum Closest, Container With Most Water, Trapping Rain Water, Sort Colors, Valid Palindrome II, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II.

Trace the tail of 'abcabcbb': at r = 5 the window is abc with l = 3. At r = 6 the new b duplicates the b at index 4, so you remove s[3] = a and s[4] = b, leaving l = 5 and window 'cb'. At r = 7 the new b duplicates index 6, so you remove c and b, leaving l = 7 and window 'b'. Best stays 3.

Linear because l and r only move forward: O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space. Optimization: keep last[c] and jump l = max(l, last[c] + 1). The max is essential: on 'abba' at r = 3 the old a was at index 0 but l is already 2; without max, l moves backward and you report 3 instead of 2.

Why shrinking from the left is safe depends on a hereditary property: if a window is valid, every sub-window of it is valid (a subset of distinct characters is still distinct; fewer distinct characters stays at most k). So when [l, r] is invalid, shrinking until valid finds the smallest l that works for this r, and for r+1 the smallest valid l can only be at least as large. That is why l never needs to move back.

With a set, shrink before inserting the new character; with a frequency map you may add first and then shrink. Cost: the while loop is nested but amortized, since each element is removed at most once, so the total is O(n). If validity needs a scan of the whole map, you lose that; maintain counters instead.

Details that decide correctness. Longest-window problems update the answer after the shrink loop. Shortest-window problems flip the structure: while the window is valid, record the answer and then shrink, so the update goes inside the loop. Use INF as the initial best and return 0 or an empty result if it is never updated.

Counting problems use a neat trick: for an 'at most k' constraint, after restoring validity every start in [l, r] yields a valid subarray ending at r, so add r - l + 1 to the count. 'Exactly k' is atMost(k) - atMost(k-1). The pseudocode runs in O(n) only if valid is O(1), meaning it relies on maintained counters, not a rescan of the window. Empty input should return 0 without touching indices.

Fixed window: maintain the aggregate incrementally, sum += a[r] - a[r-k], so total time is O(n) instead of the naive O(nk). Edge cases: k > n means there is no complete window; k = 0 is degenerate; the first k-1 positions do not yet have a full window, so start recording at r = k-1. Floating-point running sums accumulate error; use integers or recompute periodically. Sums of ints belong in 64-bit variables.

Fixed-window classics: Maximum Average Subarray I, Permutation in String (compare character counts over a window the length of the pattern; maintaining a matches counter makes each slide O(1)), Find All Anagrams. Maximum in each window is the hard sibling, because a running sum cannot be subtracted for a max; it needs a monotonic deque, giving O(n) overall.

Sliding window requires the constraint to behave monotonically as the window grows. 'Longest Subarray with Sum <= K' works only if elements are non-negative; with negatives, adding an element can decrease the sum, so shrinking is no longer the right response. Likewise Shortest Subarray with Sum >= K (LeetCode 862) allows negatives and needs prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead; a plain window fails there. Minimum Size Subarray Sum (209) has positive numbers and is fine.

Two gems: Longest Repeating Character Replacement is valid when length - maxFreq <= k, and maxFreq may stay stale because only a larger window can improve the answer. Subarray Product Less Than K needs a guard for k <= 1 (answer 0) so that l never passes r.

Stale counts: if validity is 'at most k distinct', a key whose count has dropped to 0 must be erased (or tracked by a separate distinct counter), otherwise len(map) overstates the distinct count and the window never looks valid. Answer timing: update after restoring validity for longest windows, inside the loop for shortest windows. The window length is r - l + 1, since both ends are inclusive.

Infinite loops appear when the shrink condition cannot change as l advances, usually because the removal step forgot to update the state that valid reads. Only move l inside the shrink loop, one step at a time, apart from the last-index jump guarded by max. Test: empty input, single element, all identical, all distinct, k larger than n, and k = 0.
leetcode-arrays-03.further: Use a sliding window for contiguous subarray or substring questions asking for the longest, shortest, or a count, where growing the window makes the constraint harder (or easier) in one direction. Siblings: two pointers on opposite ends (no window state, usually sorted data), prefix sums plus a hash map (the right tool when negative numbers break monotonicity), a monotonic deque (window max or min), and Kadane or DP (maximum sum without a bound). The decisive question is whether shrinking can only help. Follow-ups: Minimum Window Substring, Longest Repeating Character Replacement, Permutation in String, Sliding Window Maximum, Fruit Into Baskets, Subarrays with K Different Integers.

A stack needs only O(1) push, pop, and peek, so an array with a top index (Python list append and pop, C++ vector push_back and pop_back) is the usual implementation; a linked list also works but allocates per node. Popping or peeking an empty stack is an error or undefined behavior, so guard it.

LIFO fits nesting because the most recently opened thing must be the first to close. The call stack that runs recursion is the same idea, which is why every recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively with an explicit stack, and why very deep recursion can overflow. Related structures: queue (FIFO), deque (both ends), and the min-stack design problem, where each entry stores the value plus the minimum so far, giving O(1) getMin.

Why a stack and not just counters: with a single bracket type, a counter that never goes negative and ends at 0 is enough. With several types it is not: '([)]' has equal counts for each type but is invalid, because the nesting is wrong. The stack remembers the order of unclosed openers.

Trace '([)]': push '(', push '[', then ')' sees the top '[' which is not '(', so return false. Cheap pre-checks: an odd length can never be balanced; a string that starts with a closer fails at the first character. The end check matters too, since '(((' never fails inside the loop; only the final emptiness test catches it. The empty string is valid, since the stack is trivially empty.

Invariant, provable by induction on the prefix: at every moment the stack equals the sequence of currently unmatched openers, in order of appearance. A closer is legal only if it matches the most recent unmatched opener, which is the top, because brackets must nest rather than cross. So a mismatch or empty stack proves the string invalid, and an empty stack at the end proves it valid.

The pair map is keyed by closer, so non-bracket characters would raise KeyError in the else branch; filter them out if the input can contain letters. Relatives: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses (store the indices of unmatched characters), Longest Valid Parentheses (a stack of indices seeded with -1, O(n)), Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid (counters suffice).

A tidier variant pushes the expected closer instead of the opener: on '(' push ')', and on any closer compare directly with if not stack or stack.pop() != ch. That removes the map lookup in the else branch, and the single comparison covers both the empty and the mismatch case. Add if len(s) % 2: return False for an early exit.

The classic bugs are popping before checking emptiness (IndexError in Python, undefined behavior with std::stack::top in C++), and forgetting the final emptiness check, which lets '((' pass. Time is O(n) and space is O(n) worst case. Keep the stack of characters in a list; do not concatenate strings to emulate it, since string concatenation in a loop can degrade to O(n^2) in languages with immutable strings.

Beyond brackets: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation pushes numbers and, on an operator, pops two; the first popped is the right operand, which matters for - and /. Division should truncate toward zero, so in Python use int(a / b), because // floors negatives. Basic Calculator handles parentheses by pushing (running result, sign) on '(' and restoring on ')'. Decode String such as 3[a2[c]] uses stacks of counts and partial strings.

Iterative DFS replaces recursion with an explicit stack and avoids recursion-depth limits. Undo and redo use two stacks. Simplify Path pushes directory names and pops on '..'. Monotonic stacks (the later page) keep the stack ordered to answer next-greater questions in O(n).

Time is O(n): each character causes exactly one push or one pop attempt, and a pop only happens after a matching closer, so the total number of stack operations is at most n, each O(1). Space is O(n) in the worst case, for example n/2 openers followed by n/2 closers, where the stack peaks at n/2. For '()()()' it never exceeds 1. In general the space is O(d), where d is the maximum nesting depth.

With only one bracket type you can drop the stack for an integer counter, giving O(1) space. The recursive formulation uses the call stack instead, with the same O(d) depth, so it is no cheaper and risks stack overflow on adversarial deep input.

Empty pop: guard when a closer arrives. A string beginning with a closer must fail instantly. Unmatched opener: after the loop, a non-empty stack means failure, as with '{[()'. Mixing up which side the map is keyed on is a common slip: key by closer to look up its required opener, or push the expected closer instead.

Do not forget that '([)]' is invalid even though each pair individually appears. Use a stack of indices rather than characters whenever the answer needs positions, such as the longest valid substring. Language traps: Java's Stack class is legacy and synchronized, so prefer ArrayDeque; pop on an empty Java Stack throws EmptyStackException, while C++ std::stack::top on an empty stack is undefined behavior rather than an exception.
leetcode-stacks-01.further: Think stack when structure nests or when the newest unresolved item decides the next step: matching brackets, parsing expressions, undo history, simulating recursion, and 'next greater or smaller element'. Siblings: queue and BFS (oldest item first, level order), recursion (an implicit stack), two pointers (when no nesting memory is needed), and counters (when only one bracket type exists). Follow-ups: Min Stack, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, Daily Temperatures, Decode String, Basic Calculator, Longest Valid Parentheses, Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

With l = 0 and r = 6, mid = 0 + 6 // 2 = 3 and nums[3] = 6. The form l + (r - l) // 2 rounds toward l, so on an even-sized range it picks the lower middle. That choice has consequences: an update l = mid cannot make progress on a two-element range, while r = mid always does; if you ever need l = mid, use the upper middle, l + (r - l + 1) // 2.

Each iteration halves the range, so there are at most floor(log2 n) + 1 iterations: O(log n) time, O(1) space. The real precondition is not 'sorted' but 'a monotone predicate': the answer to some yes/no test flips exactly once across the range. An empty array gives r = -1, and the loop is skipped.

Search Insert Position asks for the lower bound: the number of elements strictly less than target, which equals the first index i with nums[i] >= target. The result lies in [0, n], not [0, n-1]: for [1, 3, 5, 6], target 7 gives 4 and target 0 gives 0. So there are n + 1 possible answers, which is why the half-open range [0, n) with r = n is the natural setup.

With duplicates, returning as soon as nums[mid] == target yields an arbitrary matching index, while the lower bound yields the leftmost. Library versions: Python bisect_left and bisect_right, C++ lower_bound and upper_bound, Java Arrays.binarySearch (returns -(insertion point) - 1 when absent). Prefer them in real code; hand-write the loop in interviews.

There are two consistent conventions. In the half-open form the range is [l, r) with r = n initially, the loop runs while l < r, the update is r = mid, and the invariant is: every index before l holds a value < target, and every index at or after r holds a value >= target. When l == r the two facts meet and l is the answer.

Termination: when l < r, mid <= r - 1, so both r = mid and l = mid + 1 shrink the range. Never mix conventions. The closed form [l, r] needs while l <= r, l = mid + 1, and r = mid - 1; pairing while l <= r with r = mid stalls when l == r == mid. In both forms the answer is l.

A classic failure: closed-range code with else: r = mid loops forever. Run nums = [1, 3, 5, 6], target = 2: mid = 1 (3 > 2) so r = 1; mid = 0 (1 < 2) so l = 1; now l = r = 1, mid = 1, 3 > 2, r = 1 again, and nothing changes. Fix A, closed range: use r = mid - 1 in the else branch (as the panel's code does); the same trace ends with r = 0, l = 1 and returns 1. Fix B, half-open: set r = len(nums), loop while l < r, and keep r = mid.

With duplicates, an early return on equality returns an arbitrary match rather than the first one, so use the lower-bound form (as in the leftmost variant) when that matters. Overflow: in Java or C++ use l + (r - l) / 2; Python integers never overflow. Total cost O(log n) comparisons.

The leftmost snippet has the same flaw as the earlier code: with while l <= r, the branch r = mid never shrinks the range at l == r. The correct closed version is r = mid - 1 in the >= branch, and it returns l, which lies in [0, n]. To test whether the target exists, check l < n and nums[l] == target.

The rightmost snippet is correct and returns r in [-1, n-1]; it equals (first index with nums[i] > target) - 1. The number of occurrences is upper_bound - lower_bound, giving the O(log n) count in a sorted array. Unified view: both are 'find the first index where a predicate becomes true', with predicate nums[i] >= t or nums[i] > t. The classic exercise is Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array.

Binary search on the answer requires a monotone feasibility test: check(x) is false for all small x and true for all large x. Example, Koko Eating Bananas: the smallest speed k with sum(ceil(p / k)) <= h, searched over [1, max(piles)]. Each check is O(n), so the total is O(n log max(piles)). Capacity to Ship Packages uses lo = max weight and hi = total weight.

Caveats: lo and hi must be guaranteed bounds, and ans = hi presumes hi is feasible; otherwise use a sentinel. To maximize instead, flip it: if check(mid), set ans = mid and lo = mid + 1. For real-valued answers, iterate a fixed 60 to 100 times instead of comparing to an epsilon. Integer square root: largest x with x <= n // x avoids overflowing x * x.

Pick one convention and memorize it. Closed: [l, r], while l <= r, l = mid + 1, r = mid - 1. Half-open: [l, r), while l < r, l = mid + 1, r = mid. Mixing them produces the infinite loops shown. The 'stuck' example in the code (l = mid with lower mid) fails when r = l + 1.

Overflow: with 32-bit ints, 2,000,000,000 + 2,000,000,000 exceeds 2,147,483,647; the midpoint bug famously sat in a widely used library implementation for years. Rotated-array searches degrade to O(n) when duplicates are allowed, because equal endpoints hide which half is sorted. Test: empty array, one element, target below the minimum, above the maximum, duplicates, and the two-element range where l and r are adjacent.
leetcode-binary-search-01.further: Use binary search when the data is sorted, or when you can define a yes/no question over an ordered range whose answer flips exactly once; 'minimum x such that...' and 'maximum feasible...' are the giveaways, as are constraints around 10^9 or 10^18. Siblings: two pointers (linear, exploits order to discard from the ends), ternary search (unimodal functions), heaps and quickselect (k-th element without full order), and plain hashing (membership only). The question to ask: can one probe at mid eliminate half the candidates? Follow-ups: Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, Find First and Last Position, Koko Eating Bananas, Capacity to Ship Packages, Median of Two Sorted Arrays.

A singly linked list is just nodes holding a value and a next pointer, with the head as the only entry point. Access by index and search are O(n); insertion or deletion right after a node you already hold is O(1). Compared with arrays, nodes cost extra memory for the pointer and have poor cache locality. A doubly linked list adds prev, giving O(1) deletion of a node you hold; an LRU cache combines a hash map with a doubly linked list for exactly that reason.

Edge cases: the empty list (head is null), a single node, and the tail's next must be null. The length is unknown up front, so counting from the end needs two passes or two pointers. In C++, free a node only after saving its next pointer.

Reversal is O(n) time and O(1) space iteratively; a recursive version uses O(n) call stack. In the recursive form, head.next.next = head; head.next = null; return newHead. Forgetting head.next = null leaves a two-node cycle at the old head. In the iterative form, the old head ends up pointing to null automatically because prev starts as null.

Related problems build on it: Reverse Linked List II (reverse positions m to n; use a dummy node, find the node before position m, reverse the segment, then reconnect both ends), Reverse Nodes in k-Group, and Palindrome Linked List (find the middle, reverse the second half, compare, optionally restore). Reversing needs no extra memory because it recycles the existing next pointers.

Order matters because overwriting curr.next before saving it makes the rest of the list unreachable. The loop invariant: prev is the head of the already reversed prefix, which ends in null, and curr is the head of the not-yet-reversed remainder; together they partition all original nodes. Each iteration moves exactly one node from the front of the remainder onto the front of the reversed part, preserving the invariant. At the end curr is null, so prev heads the fully reversed list.

In languages with parallel assignment, the compact form is curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next, but it is error-prone, so most people spell out the four steps. An empty list returns null, since prev is still null. Each node is touched once.

Trace 1 -> 2 -> 3. Start prev = null, curr = 1. Iteration 1: nxt = 2, 1.next = null, prev = 1, curr = 2. Iteration 2: nxt = 3, 2.next = 1, prev = 2, curr = 3. Iteration 3: nxt = null, 3.next = 2, prev = 3, curr = null. Return prev, which is 3, giving 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null.

Common mistakes: returning curr (always null at the end), forgetting curr = nxt (infinite loop), and using the old head afterward, since it is now the tail. For reversing part of a list, keep the node just before the segment; afterward point it at the segment's new head, and point the segment's old head (now its tail) at the node after the segment. A dummy node handles segments starting at the head.

Floyd's proof: with no cycle, fast reaches null. With a cycle of length c, fast gains one position per step on slow once both are inside it, so they meet within c steps. Time O(n), space O(1). Compare nodes by identity, not value.

To find the cycle start: let a be the distance from head to the entrance and b from the entrance to the meeting point. Slow traveled a + b and fast 2(a + b) = a + b + kc, so a = kc - b. A pointer from the head and one from the meeting point, stepping one at a time, meet at the entrance.

For an even-length list, the loop while fast and fast.next stops slow at the second middle; while fast.next and fast.next.next gives the first.

A dummy node before the head removes special cases for inserting, deleting, or merging at the head: every real node gets a predecessor, and the answer is dummy.next (the original head may have been removed).

Remove Nth Node From End, done properly: start fast and slow at the dummy, advance fast n + 1 steps, then move both until fast is null. Now slow sits on the node before the target, because the gap is exactly n + 1. Then slow.next = slow.next.next. One pass, O(L) time, O(1) space. You need the predecessor, which is the (L - n)th node counting from the dummy. If n equals the length, the head is removed, and the dummy handles that. Merging two sorted lists uses a tail pointer starting at a dummy: O(m + n).

Losing next is the signature bug: draw the boxes and after every assignment ask whether any node became unreachable. Check head, and check fast and fast.next before reading fast.next.next. Test lengths 0, 1, and 2.

Accidental cycles come from forgetting to cut a tail (set tail.next = null after splitting or reordering). Returning the wrong head is another classic; after a reversal or removal, the head is no longer the old head. In C++, deleting a node before reading its next is use-after-free.

The neat Intersection of Two Linked Lists trick has each pointer, on reaching the end, restart at the other list's head; both traverse a + b nodes and meet at the intersection or both at null, in O(m + n) with O(1) space.
leetcode-linked-lists-01.further: Think linked-list techniques when a problem says in place, O(1) extra space, kth from the end, middle, cycle, merge, or reorder nodes. Fast/slow pointers reappear on arrays as Find the Duplicate Number, where index i points to nums[i] and Floyd finds the cycle entrance. Siblings: tree problems (also pointer structures, but recursion-friendly), two pointers on arrays (same movement ideas without rewiring), and hashing (the O(n) space alternative to cycle detection). Follow-ups: Merge Two Sorted Lists, Linked List Cycle II, Reorder List, Remove Nth Node From End, Add Two Numbers, Copy List with Random Pointer, Sort List, LRU Cache, Merge k Sorted Lists.

A binary tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges and n + 1 empty child slots. Its height ranges from about log2 n (balanced) to n - 1 (a chain), and that height h governs recursion cost: O(h) stack. The 7-node example is a perfect tree of depth 2 (2^3 - 1 nodes).

Precision matters. A leaf has no children at all; a node with one child is not a leaf, which is the source of many Path Sum bugs. Depth is measured from the root, height is measured from a node down to its deepest leaf, and the height of an empty tree is -1 in edges or 0 in nodes. A binary search tree (BST) adds the rule left < node < right across the whole subtree, not just immediate children.

The orders given are correct. Inorder of a BST yields sorted values, which powers Validate BST and Kth Smallest in a BST. Preorder with null markers serializes a tree so it can be rebuilt exactly. Preorder plus inorder (distinct values) reconstruct a unique tree; preorder alone cannot. Postorder processes children before the parent, ideal for subtree aggregates such as height, size, or deletion.

All three visit every node once: O(n) time, O(h) space. Iterative inorder: push the left spine, pop and visit, then move to the right child. Morris traversal achieves O(1) space by temporarily threading pointers. Neither trick matters until recursion depth becomes a problem, which it does in Python for chains deeper than about 1000 nodes.

A reconciliation: the shown code returns the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. For this tree the path 1 -> 3 -> 6 -> 7 has 4 nodes and 3 edges, so maxDepth returns 4; the '3' in the text counts edges. LeetCode 104 counts nodes, so the answer there would be 4. Always check which convention a problem uses.

Proof by induction: depth(null) = 0, and for any node, depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). Time O(n), space O(h). For a chain of 100,000 nodes, Python raises RecursionError (default limit about 1000); use BFS counting levels, or an explicit stack of (node, depth) pairs. Minimum depth has a trap: a node with one child is not a leaf, so you cannot take the minimum of both sides when one side is null.

Count the calls: a tree with n nodes has n real calls plus n + 1 calls on null children, so 2n + 1 in total, and O(n) time. At most h + 1 frames are active at once, so stack space is O(h). Write the base case first. Reason by induction: assume dfs(child) returns the correct answer for its subtree, then decide how to combine the two results and what to return upward.

Two styles exist. Top-down passes information in parameters (remaining target sum, allowed value range), doing work before recursing. Bottom-up uses return values (height, size, found flag), doing work after the children return. Many problems combine both: Validate BST passes bounds down; Diameter returns height up. If the return value does not carry what the parent needs, return a tuple or a sentinel.

The pseudocode is the post-order bottom-up template: gather the answers from both children, combine, return. Swap the combine step and it solves a family: size is 1 + left + right, leaf count adds 1 at a leaf, Invert Binary Tree swaps the two children, Same Tree and Symmetric Tree recurse on two nodes in parallel, and Subtree of Another Tree is O(m * n) with the naive approach.

In C++, null should be nullptr. Time O(n); space O(h). A BFS level count computes the same value iteratively. An explicit stack of (node, depth) pairs also works and avoids recursion limits. Raising Python's recursion limit with sys.setrecursionlimit is risky for very deep trees, since the interpreter itself can crash when the C stack runs out, so prefer an iterative version for chains.

Path Sum: check the leaf condition. For tree [1, 2] and target 1, the root has a child so it is not a leaf and the answer is false; treating a null child as a leaf would wrongly say true. With negative values, never prune on overshoot. Balanced tree: recomputing height at every node is O(n^2) on a chain; the efficient post-order returns the height, or -1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced, giving O(n).

LCA works because each call answers 'did I find p or q in this subtree?'; when both sides answer yes, this node is the split point. It assumes both p and q exist. In a BST, LCA uses ordering and takes O(h). Diameter and Maximum Path Sum return a one-branch value upward while updating a best answer using both branches.

Global state: a shared best variable is fine when needed (Diameter, Maximum Path Sum), but reset it per call and keep it local or nonlocal; stale globals break repeated test cases. Prefer return values when they suffice. Null checks always come first.

BST validation trap: comparing a node only with its parent fails on [5, 1, 6, null, null, 4, 7], since 4 is in the right subtree of 5 yet smaller than 5; pass (low, high) bounds down. Use None or infinity for the initial bounds rather than INT_MIN, because node values can equal INT_MIN. Compare nodes by identity, not value, in LCA when values repeat. Convention errors (edges versus nodes, depth versus level) cost more points than any algorithmic mistake, so restate the definition from the examples before coding.
leetcode-trees-01.further: Think tree DFS whenever the data is hierarchical, the question is for every node or every root-to-leaf path, or the answer for a node is built from its children's answers. Siblings: BFS (level order, nearest, minimum depth), backtracking (DFS that mutates and undoes shared state), tree DP (DFS returning several values per node), and graph DFS (same recursion plus a visited set). A useful test is top-down versus bottom-up: do I pass information down, or return it up? Follow-ups: Invert Binary Tree, Diameter of Binary Tree, Validate BST, Lowest Common Ancestor, Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder, Serialize and Deserialize.

Use a real queue: Python collections.deque with popleft, Java ArrayDeque, C++ std::queue. Python list.pop(0) is O(n) and turns BFS into O(n^2).

The frontier invariant: after finishing level k, the queue holds exactly level k + 1, in left-to-right order. Time is O(n) because each node is enqueued and dequeued once. Space is O(w), where w is the widest level, up to about n / 2 for a complete tree's last level. That contrasts with DFS, which needs O(h): a bushy balanced tree is cheaper for DFS, while a chain is cheaper for BFS (the queue holds one node, but a recursive DFS would have n frames).

In the example, levels are [3], [9, 20], [15, 7]; the queue never holds more than two nodes at once.

Why level_size works: at the top of each outer iteration, the queue contains exactly one level. Snapshot its length, dequeue exactly that many nodes, and the children they enqueue sit behind them and belong to the next level. Alternatives: store (node, depth) pairs, or keep two lists, current and next. The empty-tree guard is required, since enqueueing null would crash on node.val; the answer for an empty tree is [], not [[]].

Time O(n); space O(w) plus O(n) for the output. Variants with tiny edits: Right Side View (last value of each level), Zigzag Level Order (reverse every other level's list), Average of Levels, Connect Next Right Pointers, and Minimum Depth (return at the first leaf dequeued, which can finish early on wide trees).

The input [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] is the level-order serialization used by LeetCode, with nulls for missing children; the children of a null are not listed, so index arithmetic like 2i + 1 does not apply. It only applies to the complete-tree array layout used by heaps.

Trace: queue [3]. Level size 1: dequeue 3, enqueue 9 and 20, level [3]. Size 2: dequeue 9 (no children), dequeue 20 and enqueue 15 and 7, level [9, 20]. Size 2: dequeue 15 and 7, level [15, 7]. Output [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]. The number of levels equals height + 1. Edge cases: a single node gives [[x]]; a chain gives one value per level.

DFS uses a stack or recursion and O(h) memory; BFS uses a queue and O(w) memory. Both visit every node and edge once, so each is O(V + E) on a graph. The difference is order, and BFS's order guarantees fewest edges.

Proof sketch: the queue always holds nodes at distance d followed by nodes at distance d + 1, never more than two consecutive values, in nondecreasing order. So a node is first discovered through a shortest path. DFS can find a path but not necessarily the shortest.

Add edge weights and the guarantee breaks: use Dijkstra with a heap; with weights only 0 and 1, a deque-based 0-1 BFS works. DFS is not the only way to topologically sort: Kahn's algorithm is a BFS-style method driven by indegrees.

The correct invariant for shortest paths is that nodes leave the queue in nondecreasing distance, and it relies on marking a node visited when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued. Multi-source BFS starts with all sources in the queue at distance 0 and runs once in O(V + E), instead of once per source: Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix, and Walls and Gates are all this.

State-space BFS treats puzzle configurations as nodes: Word Ladder, Open the Lock, Sliding Puzzle; encode a state as a string or tuple so it is hashable. Bidirectional BFS searches from both ends and meets in the middle, cutting roughly b^d work to 2 * b^(d/2) when the branching factor b is large. Level aggregates fall out of the level_size loop.

The level-mixing bug appears only if you read the size after enqueueing; take it before the loop starts. Tree BFS needs no visited set, because every node has one parent and is reachable by exactly one path. Graph and grid BFS do need one. Mark visited on enqueue; marking on dequeue lets the same node enter the queue several times before it is processed, wasting time and sometimes memory.

Other traps: list.pop(0) in Python; not guarding null children; reading from an empty queue; bounds checks on grids. If you test for the target on discovery rather than on dequeue you save a level of work. Counting steps: increment a counter after each completed level, or store dist alongside the node. Off-by-one is common: decide whether the start is level 0 or 1 from the problem's examples.
leetcode-trees-02.further: Choose BFS for anything described in layers: level-order output, minimum number of steps or moves in an unweighted graph or grid, nearest target, or a process that spreads in rounds (infection, fire, rotting). Siblings: DFS (any path, all paths, components, memory O(h)), Dijkstra (weighted shortest path, a heap instead of a plain queue), 0-1 BFS, Kahn's topological sort (BFS on indegrees), and union-find (connectivity only, no paths). Decide by the question: minimum steps points to BFS, existence or enumeration to DFS. Follow-ups: Right Side View, Zigzag Level Order, Rotting Oranges, Word Ladder, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix, 01 Matrix, Minimum Depth, Open the Lock.

Children can be a dict (memory proportional to the children that actually exist) or a fixed array of 26 pointers (direct indexing, but about 208 bytes per node on a 64-bit machine, mostly null). A trie holds at most 1 + (total characters inserted) nodes, and prefix sharing makes it fewer.

The isEnd flag is independent of having children: 'app' is a word and also a prefix of 'apple', so a node can be terminal and still have children. The root represents the empty prefix, so inserting the empty string sets root.isEnd. Optional extras per node: a pass-through counter for prefix counts, or the stored word at terminal nodes. A hash set also takes O(L) to hash a word but cannot answer prefix queries without scanning.

search and startsWith differ only in the last line: isEnd versus path-exists. With only 'apple' inserted, search('app') is False (the node after the second p has isEnd False) and startsWith('app') is True. Inserting 'app' later just flips that flag, and inserting the same word twice changes nothing.

In Python, node.children.setdefault(ch, Node()) shortens insertion but allocates a Node on every call; check membership first if allocation matters. Deletion is rare in interviews: unmark isEnd, then prune upward every node that has no children and is not terminal. The key property is that each operation costs O(L) regardless of how many words are stored. A sorted array with binary search costs O(L log n) per lookup, because each comparison itself can take O(L).

A trie shares prefixes only. 'bat' and 'cat' end in the same suffix 'at', but they get separate branches; merging suffixes is a different structure (a DAWG). Here the stored words app, appl, apple, bat, cat use 1 root + 5 nodes (a, p, p, l, e) + 3 + 3 = 12 nodes for 18 total characters, with terminal flags on the second p, the l, the e, and both t nodes. Notice 'appl' ends mid-path, exactly why the flag is separate from leaf-ness.

Walking children in alphabetical order with DFS lists all words in lexicographic order, which is how tries support sorted enumeration. The shape does not depend on insertion order, because each node's identity is determined by its prefix string.

The invariant: the node reached by following the characters of w from the root represents the prefix w, and its isEnd is True exactly when w was inserted as a word. Everything else follows. All three operations stop early when a child is missing, and all three are O(L) in the length of the query, with no dependence on the dictionary size.

Useful variants of the same walk: count words with a given prefix (store a pass-through counter incremented during insert); longest common prefix of many words (walk while the current node has exactly one child and is not terminal); autocomplete (walk to the prefix node, then DFS its subtree to collect completions); and Add and Search Words with a '.' wildcard (at a '.', recurse into every child, which can visit the whole trie in the worst case).

O(L) assumes O(1) access to a child (array index or hash lookup). Building a trie from words with T total characters costs O(T). Space is at most O(T) nodes, multiplied by the per-node child storage: 26 slots per node with arrays, or hash-table overhead with dicts. The length of the dictionary n does not appear in the per-operation cost, which is the strength of the structure.

Compare with a hash set: expected O(L) to hash, but it answers only exact membership. If words share almost nothing, a trie uses far more memory than a set. For large alphabets such as Unicode, use dicts or a radix tree. A sorted array can also answer prefix queries (binary search for the lower and upper bounds of the prefix) with much less memory.

Word Search II: insert all words into a trie, then DFS from each board cell while following trie children, pruning as soon as the path has no trie continuation. This replaces W separate board searches. When a word is found, record it once and clear its flag (or prune the now-useless leaf) to avoid duplicates and speed later searches.

Other uses: Replace Words, Longest Word in Dictionary, Search Suggestions System, and Design Search Autocomplete System (ranking needs counts stored per node). A binary trie over bits solves Maximum XOR of Two Numbers: for each x, walk 31 levels and greedily take the opposite bit when it exists, O(31 n) overall. IP routing tables use longest-prefix matching on a binary radix trie. Aho-Corasick adds failure links to a trie to search many patterns in text at once.

The speed comes at a memory cost. A Python object per node can cost hundreds of bytes, so a million nodes may mean hundreds of megabytes; 26-slot arrays waste most slots on sparse data. Mitigations: dict children for sparse alphabets, a radix (compressed) tree that collapses single-child chains so n words need at most about 2n nodes, or a DAWG that also shares suffixes.

When not to use a trie: you only need exact membership (use a set), you need sorted order or range queries over whole keys (a sorted array or balanced tree), or the data set is small. Tries shine when queries are prefix-heavy and read-heavy. They are also cache-unfriendly, because every step is a pointer hop to a node that may be anywhere in memory.

Forgetting to set isEnd on the last node is the classic bug: every word then looks like a mere prefix. Character mapping: an index like ord(c) - ord('a') silently breaks on uppercase letters, digits, or punctuation, producing negative or out-of-range indexes. Normalize case if the problem says so, and use a dict when the alphabet is not guaranteed.

In Python, never give a node a shared mutable default, such as a children dict defined as a default argument or class attribute; every node would share one dict. Handle the empty string and duplicates explicitly. In Word Search II, use a visited marker on the board cell during DFS and restore it afterward, and deduplicate results. In C++, give the trie a destructor, or you leak every node.
leetcode-trees-03.further: Think trie when many queries concern prefixes of strings from a fixed dictionary: autocomplete, spell checking, prefix counts, longest common prefix, or pruning a board search with many target words. Siblings: hash set (exact membership only), sorted array plus binary search (prefix range, little memory), suffix array or suffix automaton (substring queries), Aho-Corasick (many patterns searched inside one text), and radix tree (a space-efficient trie). Decide by the query type: prefix means trie; arbitrary substring means a suffix structure. Follow-ups: Implement Trie, Design Add and Search Words, Word Search II, Replace Words, Search Suggestions System, Maximum XOR of Two Numbers, Palindrome Pairs.

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array: children of index i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, the parent at (i - 1) // 2. Peek is O(1); push (sift up) and pop (sift down) are O(log n); building a heap from an array with heapify is O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and sift only a few levels.

A heap only orders parent against child, not siblings, so it is not sorted and cannot search for an arbitrary value faster than O(n). Both example trees satisfy their rules. Python's heapq was min-only until Python 3.14 added heappush_max and related max-heap functions (on older versions, store negated keys); Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; C++ priority_queue is a max-heap by default.

Why a min-heap finds the largest: the heap keeps the k largest values seen so far, and its root is the smallest of those k, which is exactly the k-th largest overall. Duplicates count separately: for [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6] and k = 4 the answer is 4 (descending: 6, 5, 5, 4). Assume k <= n; k = 1 is the maximum and k = n the minimum.

Alternatives and trade-offs: sorting is O(n log n); quickselect is O(n) on average but O(n^2) worst case and mutates the array; heapifying everything and popping k times costs O(n + k log n); the size-k heap costs O(n log k) time and only O(k) space, and it works on streams where you cannot store the data, as in Kth Largest Element in a Stream.

Trace with k = 2: the first two elements fill the heap as {2, 3}, root 2. Then 1 is not greater than 2, so it is ignored; 5 replaces 2, giving {3, 5}; 6 replaces 3, giving {5, 6}; 4 is not greater than 5 and is ignored. The final root is 5, the second largest.

Invariant: after each element, the heap holds the k largest elements of the prefix. An element not larger than the root cannot belong to the top k of the prefix, and since the prefix's top k only grows more demanding, it can never matter later. Ties with the root can be ignored without changing the value. In Python, heapq.heapreplace fuses pop and push into one O(log k) step.

Edge cases: if k > n the heap never fills and peek returns the overall minimum, which is wrong; validate k. An empty array has no answer. Cost analysis: each of the n elements does one O(1) comparison, and at most one replace of O(log k). Worst case is increasing input, where every element replaces the root: O(n log k). Best case is decreasing input, where after the first k nothing enters: about O(n + k log k). Space is O(k). Using the library, heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1] does the same in O(n log k).

Why log k and not log n: the heap never grows beyond k elements, so its height is floor(log2 k), and each sift touches at most that many levels. If k is a constant, the whole algorithm is O(n); if k is close to n, it degrades to O(n log n), no better than sorting, and quickselect becomes attractive.

A lower bound note: any comparison-based selection needs at least about n comparisons, since every element must be inspected, so the O(n) of quickselect (or median-of-medians in the worst case) is the theoretical optimum. The heap is the right tool when elements arrive online, memory is limited, or the data must not be mutated. For the k-th smallest, mirror the idea with a size-k max-heap. If you also need the top k in sorted order, add O(k log k).

Top K Frequent Elements: count in O(n), then keep a size-k min-heap by frequency, O(n log k); bucket sort by frequency gives O(n). Merge k sorted lists: the heap holds one head per list, and each of the N total elements is popped and replaced once, so O(N log k) time and O(k) space; merging lists one after another costs O(Nk). The shown example merges to 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9. In Python, tuples (value, node) fail on ties because nodes are not comparable; add a unique index: (value, i, node).

More uses: Meeting Rooms II (min-heap of end times), Dijkstra (heap of (distance, node) with lazy deletion), and Find Median from Data Stream (max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper, sizes within one).

Direction: kth largest uses a min-heap of size k; kth smallest uses a max-heap of size k. Keep the size at most k. Heaps do not support decrease-key or removing an arbitrary element efficiently: use lazy deletion (leave stale entries and skip them when popped) or re-push with a new priority. Mutating an object's priority while it sits in the heap silently breaks the invariant.

Iterating over the underlying list does not give sorted order; only repeated pops do. In C++, negating INT_MIN overflows, so use a comparator instead of negation. Python max-heaps via negation are fine. Ties need a deterministic tie-breaker if items are not comparable. The k-th largest is index k - 1 in descending order, so check off-by-one. For the k-th largest distinct value, deduplicate with a set first.

Siblings: sorting (everything in order, O(n log n)), quickselect (one k-th element, O(n) average), monotonic deque (extreme of a sliding window in O(n)), balanced BST or sorted container (arbitrary deletes and neighbor queries), and bucket sort (bounded integer keys). Follow-ups: Kth Largest Element in a Stream, Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points to Origin, Merge k Sorted Lists, Find Median from Data Stream, Task Scheduler, Last Stone Weight.

Backtracking is a depth-first search over an implicit tree of partial solutions: the tree is generated by the choices, not stored. The defining discipline is that every change to the shared state is reversed when the call returns, so each frame sees the state exactly as its parent left it.

It differs from plain DFS on an explicit graph because of that undo step, and from dynamic programming (DP) in what it does with repeated work. Backtracking walks every path, so it is the tool when you must output all solutions. If you only need a count or an optimum and different paths reach the same remaining subproblem, memoization (DP) merges them and wins exponentially. Recursion depth equals the number of decisions, which is usually small enough for the call stack.

There are 2^n subsets, and the average size is n / 2, so any enumeration needs Omega(n * 2^n) work just to write the output; the standard solution is O(n * 2^n) because each recorded subset is copied. The include/exclude tree has 2^(n+1) - 1 nodes and 2^n leaves. The popular for-loop formulation (choose a next index at or after start) records a subset at every node instead, so it has just 2^n nodes.

That version produces [], [1], [1,2], [1,2,3], [1,3], [2], [2,3], [3], not the size-sorted list shown. For input with duplicates (Subsets II), sort first and skip a value equal to its predecessor at the same level: if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue. A bitmask loop over 0 to 2^n - 1 is an iterative alternative for small n.

The invariant: on entering backtrack(state), the state contains exactly the choices made along the path from the root; on returning, it is restored to what it was on entry. By induction this holds if each choose is paired with an unchoose and each recursive call obeys the same rule. Record solutions as copies, since the path object keeps changing.

Fit the template to the problem. Permutations use a used array or in-place swaps. Combinations and subsets use a start index so that choices only move forward, which prevents counting {1, 2} and {2, 1} as different. For existence questions (Sudoku, Word Search), return True up the stack to short-circuit as soon as one solution is found. Always put the solution check before the loop, and choose the order of candidates so that the most constrained decisions come first.

Permutations have n! leaves; with copying, O(n * n!). For duplicate inputs (Permutations II), sort and skip a value equal to its predecessor when the predecessor is not currently used. Combinations number C(n, k); C(5, 3) = 10, matching the list. Prune loops with i <= n - (k - len(path)) + 1 so that you never start a branch that cannot reach size k. Combination Sum, where an element may be reused, recurses with the same index.

N-Queens: there are 2 solutions for n = 4 and 92 for n = 8. Place one queen per row, so rows never conflict, and keep sets for columns and for the two diagonal families (r - c and r + c) to test a square in O(1). Others: Word Search, Palindrome Partitioning, Generate Parentheses, Sudoku.

Pruning keeps the result identical but can shrink the search by orders of magnitude; it does not change the exponential worst case in general. Types: feasibility pruning (a constraint is already violated), bound pruning (even the best completion cannot beat the best answer so far, called branch and bound), duplicate and symmetry skipping, and ordering heuristics that fail early.

Soundness is the rule: prune only when no valid solution can lie in that subtree. Example, Combination Sum: sort the candidates, then stop the loop when a candidate exceeds the remaining target, since every later candidate is at least as large. In N-Queens, the column and diagonal sets are what reduce the n^n raw placements toward something far smaller. A pruning test must be cheap relative to the work it saves, or it makes things slower.

The b^d estimate is nodes explored, multiplied by the work per node. Concrete anchors: subsets O(n * 2^n), permutations O(n * n!), and a fully branching tree with b = 2 and d = 30 already has about a billion leaves. Practical limits: 2^n is feasible up to n of about 20 to 25, and n! up to roughly 10 or 11 (10! is 3.6 million, 12! is 479 million).

Space excluding output is O(d) for the recursion plus the path. If different paths lead to the same remaining state, as in Word Break or Partition Equal Subset Sum, memoize and the problem becomes DP with polynomial states. To bound a solution, count leaves and multiply by the cost per leaf; if the count exceeds about 10^8, look for a smarter idea instead of micro-optimizing.

The shared-path bug: output.append(path) stores a reference, so later mutations change saved results, and at the end every entry becomes the same (usually empty) list. Copy at record time: path[:] or list(path). Forgetting to undo leaks state into sibling branches. A subtler variant is returning early between choose and unchoose, for example an early return placed after choosing; use structure that guarantees the undo, or restore before returning.

Strings are immutable, so passing path + ch as an argument needs no undo, at the price of copying. Do not mutate a list you are iterating over. Duplicates in the input generate duplicate outputs unless you sort and skip. In Python, recursion deeper than about 1000 frames raises RecursionError, which matters for grid searches. Keep counters local to a call, not global across test cases.

Add a few decisions to the checklist. Pick a compact state: an index, a remaining target, a bitmask. Decide the return type up front: collect all solutions, count them, return a boolean to short-circuit, or track a best value with pruning. Estimate the number of leaves before coding to check feasibility.

Tiny cases to test: n = 0, where subsets and permutations should return [[]] (one empty arrangement), not []; n = 1; all-duplicate input; and inputs with no solution, where the result should be empty rather than an error. Add a debug print on entry and exit to confirm the path is restored. If a candidate appears multiple times in the output, you probably forgot the start index or the duplicate skip. Finally, check that your base case also handles a solution reached with no remaining choices.
leetcode-backtracking-01.further: Use backtracking when the problem says generate all, list every, or find any arrangement that satisfies constraints, and the input is small (n up to roughly 20) or heavily constrained. Siblings: plain DFS on a graph or tree (no undo needed, no enumeration of paths), dynamic programming (counts or optima when subproblems repeat), greedy (one provably safe choice, no search), and BFS (fewest steps). The key test: must you output every solution, or only a number? If only a number and states repeat, memoize instead. Follow-ups: Permutations, Combination Sum, Subsets II, Palindrome Partitioning, N-Queens, Word Search, Generate Parentheses, Sudoku Solver.

This graph has V = 6 vertices and E = 8 edges. In an undirected graph the degrees sum to 2E = 16, which checks out: 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2. A simple undirected graph (no loops or repeated edges) has at most V(V-1)/2 = 15 edges, so this one is fairly dense for its size.

Representation trade-off: an adjacency list uses O(V + E) space and iterates a vertex's neighbors in O(degree); an adjacency matrix uses O(V^2) space but answers 'is there an edge?' in O(1). Interviews default to lists. Watch the labeling: vertices 1..6 need arrays of size V + 1. Many problems give an implicit graph (grid cells, word ladders, puzzle states) where you generate neighbors on the fly and never build lists. Also handle self-loops, parallel edges, and disconnected graphs.

When building from an edge list, an undirected edge must be added in both directions; adding it once silently produces a directed graph, and then traversals miss nodes. Use defaultdict(list) or preallocate V + 1 lists so isolated vertices still have an entry.

In the directed example, everything is reachable from 1: 1 reaches 2 and 3, 2 reaches 4, 3 reaches 5, and 4 reaches 6. The order in which DFS or BFS visits vertices depends on neighbor order, but the set of reachable vertices does not. For weighted graphs store (neighbor, weight) pairs. To walk edges backward (needed for some problems), build the reversed graph. Total memory is O(V + E), and the sum of list lengths is E for directed graphs and 2E for undirected ones.

Counting 1-regions: scan every cell, and each time you meet an unvisited land cell, increment the count and flood the whole component. This is correct because components partition the land cells, so each is counted exactly once. The answer 5 is: top-left group, the top-right group, the middle-bottom group, the lone cell at row 3 column 0, and the lone cell at row 4 column 4. Time is O(m * n) since each cell is processed a constant number of times; extra space is O(m * n) in the worst case for the stack, queue, or visited set.

With 8-directional adjacency the same grid has only 3 islands, because diagonals join the right-hand groups. Edge cases: empty grid, all water (0), all land (1). Union-Find handles the dynamic variant where land is added over time.

DFS and BFS find exactly the same set; choose by convenience. Bounds check comes first (0 <= r < m and 0 <= c < n), then the cell test; a direction list like [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)] keeps the code short. Mark a cell the moment you discover it (push or enqueue it), not when you pop it. With iterative DFS, marking on pop is still correct but can push the same cell several times.

In-place marking, turning '1' into '0', saves the visited structure but destroys the input, and fails in languages where the grid is immutable, so state the trade-off. Flood Fill (the problem) has a trap: if the new color equals the old one, naive recursion never terminates, so return early. Relatives: Max Area of Island, Surrounded Regions, and Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (search inward from the borders).

Complexity O(V + E): every vertex is enqueued or visited once, and each adjacency list is scanned once. For undirected graphs each edge appears in two lists, which is still O(E). Space is O(V) for the visited set plus O(V) for the queue or recursion, since depth can reach V.

One traversal only covers the start vertex's component. To cover the whole graph, add an outer loop over all vertices and start a new traversal at each unvisited one; the total remains O(V + E). In directed graphs a plain visited set answers reachability but not cycle detection, which needs per-node states (see the next topic's three-color method). For dense integer labels, a boolean array beats a set. On grids, use a boolean matrix or mark in place.

The six-vertex graph drawn above is connected (edges 2-4, 2-5 and 3-5 bridge the two triples), so it has one component; removing those three cross edges would leave {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6}. The shortest path from 1 to 5 has length 2 (1-2-5 or 1-3-5), and BFS reports 2.

Component counting uses an outer loop of traversals, or Union-Find with near-constant amortized cost per union. BFS gives distances from the source to every vertex in O(V + E) and a parent map reconstructs the path. If edges have weights, use Dijkstra (nonnegative) or Bellman-Ford (negatives allowed). For directed graphs, 'connected' splits into weak versus strong connectivity; strongly connected components need Tarjan's or Kosaraju's algorithm.

Without a visited set, any cycle loops forever, and in an undirected graph every edge is a two-cycle (u to v and back to u). Grid mutation versus extra space is a design choice to state aloud. Recursion depth is the real danger: a 300 by 300 all-land grid can recurse about 90,000 deep, but Python's default limit is 1000 and a JVM thread typically manages tens of thousands. Switch to an iterative stack or queue; raising Python's limit can crash the interpreter.

Other traps: marking visited at dequeue time in BFS (duplicates in the queue multiply work), forgetting the outer loop on disconnected graphs, building undirected edges one way, confusing 0-indexed and 1-indexed labels, and mixing '1' strings with 1 integers in grid input.
leetcode-graphs-01.further: Think graph traversal when the problem talks about connectivity, reachability, regions, components, dependencies, relationships, or the fewest moves; a grid, a set of states, or words differing by one letter are implicit graphs. Siblings: Union-Find (connectivity under merges, no paths), topological sort (ordering a DAG), Dijkstra (weighted shortest paths), tree traversals (no visited set needed), and grid DP (counts or optima where moves only go right or down, which is acyclic). Pick BFS for fewest steps, DFS or BFS for components. Follow-ups: Max Area of Island, Clone Graph, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow, Surrounded Regions, Rotting Oranges, Number of Provinces, Graph Valid Tree, Word Ladder.

With the convention that u -> v means u must come first, the diagram has eight edges: A to B and C; B to D and E; C to F; and D, E, F to G. A topological order is a listing of all vertices in which every edge points forward, and one exists if and only if the graph is a DAG. Many orders exist: A, B, C, D, E, F, G and A, C, F, B, E, D, G are both valid.

Edge direction is the top source of bugs, so fix one convention. In LeetCode's Course Schedule, a pair [a, b] means b comes before a, i.e. edge b -> a. In a DAG the longest path, counted in vertices, is the minimum number of parallel rounds; here it is 4 (A, B, D, G).

This panel shows how the input maps to edges. LeetCode lists pairs [course, prerequisite], so each pair [B, A] becomes the edge A -> B. If you instead store course -> prerequisites and run Kahn's algorithm on it directly, indegree counts how many courses depend on a node, so the first vertex removed is G, and the output is a reversed schedule. Either reverse the result or build the graph as prerequisite -> course. Cycle detection gives the same verdict either way.

Here G has three prerequisites, D, E and F, which the indegree trace uses. Isolated vertices must still be counted in V, and duplicate edges are fine as long as indegree and decrements stay consistent.

Starting from queue [A]: pop A, giving B and C indegree 0, queue [B, C]. Pop B, queue [C, D, E]. Pop C, queue [D, E, F], order [A, B, C]. Pop D (G: 3 to 2), pop E (G: 2 to 1), pop F (G: 0, joins queue), pop G. Final order [A, B, C, D, E, F, G].

Why it works: a removed vertex has no unfinished prerequisites. In a DAG, some remaining vertex always has indegree 0, since following predecessors backward forever would eventually repeat a vertex and form a cycle. So the process consumes everything. With a cycle, the cycle's vertices and everything downstream never reach indegree 0, so the order ends shorter than V. Time and space are O(V + E).

Implementation traps. queue.pop(0) on a Python list costs O(n); use collections.deque and popleft. The indegree dict requires every vertex to be a key of graph, including vertices that only appear as neighbors, otherwise KeyError. The comment in the code says neighbors are prerequisites, but the algorithm needs graph[u] to hold the dependents, the vertices that must come after u. Returning [] for a cycle is ambiguous with an empty graph; Course Schedule just returns a boolean.

Variants: to get the lexicographically smallest order, replace the queue with a min-heap (O((V + E) log V)). Processing level by level gives the minimum number of rounds (Parallel Courses). Alien Dictionary builds edges from adjacent words and must reject the case where a longer word precedes its own prefix, such as abc before ab.

GRAY marks vertices on the current DFS path, so an edge into a GRAY vertex is a back edge, which exists exactly when the directed graph has a cycle. An edge into a BLACK vertex reaches finished work and is harmless. That is why one visited flag is wrong for directed graphs: in the diamond A -> B, A -> C, B -> D, C -> D, vertex D is reached twice without any cycle.

A self-loop u -> u is caught because u is GRAY when examined. Reverse finishing order (when vertices turn BLACK) is a valid topological order. Time O(V + E); recursion depth up to V, so go iterative for large inputs. For undirected graphs the rule differs: an edge to a visited vertex that is not the parent signals a cycle, or use Union-Find.

A DAG may have many topological orders; the order is unique exactly when the Kahn queue holds a single vertex at every step. Real systems built on this: build tools such as make and Bazel, package managers, spreadsheet recalculation (a cell's formula inputs must be computed first), and task schedulers.

A powerful follow-on: shortest or longest paths on a DAG are solvable in O(V + E) by relaxing edges in topological order, even with negative weights, which beats Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford; counting the number of paths works the same way. If the graph may contain cycles, compress each strongly connected component (Tarjan or Kosaraju) into one node, and the result is always a DAG. Sequence Reconstruction asks whether the topological order is unique, which is the single-vertex-queue test.

Edge direction first: re-derive 'which way does the arrow point' from a two-node example before coding. Cycle handling: compare the length of the order to V, never to the number of edges. In Course Schedule, V is numCourses, not the number of prerequisite pairs, so courses with no prerequisites still count. Self-loops, duplicate edges, isolated nodes, and several disconnected components should all be tested.

Detecting a cycle is different from reporting one: to return an actual cycle, track parent pointers in DFS and walk back from the GRAY target. Recursion depth is a risk in the DFS version. If a cycle exists, say clearly that no valid order exists, rather than returning a partial order. Finally, do not confuse this with undirected problems like Graph Valid Tree, where Union-Find or a parent-aware DFS is the right tool.
leetcode-graphs-02.further: Use topological ideas whenever a problem has prerequisites, dependencies, or before/after constraints and asks for an order, a feasibility check, or the number of rounds. Siblings: plain DFS or BFS (reachability without ordering), Union-Find (undirected connectivity and cycles), Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall (weighted shortest paths), and minimum spanning trees (cheapest way to connect everything). Quick split: dependencies mean topological sort; cheapest route means Dijkstra; cheapest connection means MST. Follow-ups: Course Schedule I and II, Alien Dictionary, Parallel Courses, Minimum Height Trees, Find All Possible Recipes, Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights Within K Stops.
