The recipe works because of two properties: optimal substructure (the best answer for the whole is built from best answers for parts) and overlapping subproblems (the same parts recur). For House Robber, the plain recursion f(i) = max(f(i-1), f(i-2) + a[i]) is exponential, roughly 1.618^n, like naive Fibonacci, because the same f values are recomputed. Memoizing it creates only n distinct subproblems at O(1) each, so O(n).

Top-down (memoized recursion) is easier to derive; bottom-up avoids recursion limits and allows space compression. Define the state exactly: 'best using houses 0..i' is a different state from 'best that robs house i', and the final answer extraction differs (dp[n-1] versus max over all dp). Prove correctness by induction on i.

Why not brute force: the number of valid subsets with no two adjacent houses grows like Fibonacci, exponentially. Why not greedy (take the biggest house, then the biggest allowed): on [5, 6, 5] greedy takes 6 and is stuck with 6, while robbing both 5s gives 10.

Edge cases: an empty array returns 0, one house returns nums[0], two houses return the larger one. The recurrence handles all of them if the two rolling values start at 0. Variants: House Robber II (houses in a circle): the first and last are adjacent, so return max(rob(nums[0..n-2]), rob(nums[1..n-1])), with n = 1 as a special case. House Robber III (a tree): a DFS returning a (rob this node, skip this node) pair. Delete and Earn reduces to House Robber after summing values by number.

The optimum of 12 comes from houses 0, 2, and 4: 2 + 9 + 1 (houses 1 and 2 are adjacent, so 7 + 9 = 16 is not allowed). Competing choices are all worse: houses 1 and 3 give 10, houses 1 and 4 give 8, houses 0 and 3 give 5.

To recover which houses, keep the whole prefix table: dp = [2, 7, 11, 11, 12]. Walk backward from the end: at index 4, dp[4] = 12 differs from dp[3] = 11, so house 4 was taken; jump to index 2, where 11 differs from dp[1] = 7, so take house 2; jump to index 0, take house 0. If dp[i] equals dp[i-1], house i was skipped. The O(1)-space version cannot do this reconstruction, which is its one cost.

Proof of the recurrence, with dp[i] defined as the best total using houses 0..i only. An optimal solution either skips house i, which leaves an optimal solution for houses 0..i-1, worth dp[i-1], or takes house i, which forbids house i-1 and leaves an optimal solution for houses 0..i-2, worth dp[i-2] + nums[i]. The cases are exhaustive, so the maximum is correct. Base values: dp[-1] = dp[-2] = 0, meaning nothing to rob.

Notice that dp[i-1] may or may not include house i-1; it is the best over the whole prefix, which is why dp is nondecreasing. The alternative state 'best that robs i' needs a max over all j <= i-2 and is clumsier. Computed table for the example: [2, 7, 11, 11, 12]. Time O(n), space O(n) with the array.

Only two earlier values are ever read, so memory drops from O(n) to O(1). The classic update bug is writing prev1 = curr before prev2 = prev1, so prev2 ends up equal to curr; the tuple assignment prev2, prev1 = prev1, curr avoids it by evaluating the right side first.

Starting both values at 0 represents the empty prefix and a nonexistent house before the first, so n = 0 returns 0 and n = 1 returns nums[0] with no special cases. General rule: if the recurrence reads the last k states, keep k variables; if it can read any earlier state (as Longest Increasing Subsequence does), the table cannot be compressed this way. You also give up reconstruction of the chosen items, unless you store decisions separately.

Quick tests, tracing the code: [] gives 0; [5] gives 5; [2, 1, 1, 2] gives 4, taking houses 0 and 3 (steps: 2, 2, 3, 4); [1, 2, 3, 1] gives 4; [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] gives 12. Time O(n), space O(1).

Large totals: with many houses and big values, sums need 64-bit integers in C++ or Java; Python handles it. The values here are nonnegative. If negatives were allowed, the max with the skip branch already keeps the answer from dropping below 0, since robbing nothing is permitted. Style: curr = max(take, skip) is clearer than the conditional. The scan reads each number once, so this is optimal up to constants: any correct algorithm must look at every house.

Include or exclude is the general shape: each element is either used or not, with a constraint tying neighboring choices together. Siblings: Climbing Stairs (dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], counting rather than maximizing; the answer is Fibonacci F(n+1), which exceeds a 32-bit int at n = 46), Min Cost Climbing Stairs, Decode Ways (count valid one- and two-digit splits, careful with zeros), Coin Change (dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - c], O(amount * coins), initialize with infinity not 0), Maximum Subarray (Kadane: best ending here = max(x, best + x)), and Longest Increasing Subsequence (O(n^2), or O(n log n) with a tails array).

Wrong base cases: for i = 1, dp[i-2] is dp[-1], which in Python silently reads the last element. Pad the array or use rolling variables. Initial value of zero is wrong for 'maximum' when all values may be negative and you must take at least one (Kadane needs the first element or negative infinity). Min problems need an infinity sentinel that will not overflow when you add to it.

State confusion: if dp[i] means 'ending exactly at i', the answer is the max over all dp, not dp[n-1]. Counting problems often ask for the result modulo 10^9 + 7, so reduce after each addition. Top-down solutions can hit the recursion limit near n of about 1000 in Python. Over-building the table costs memory, not correctness.
leetcode-dp-01.further: Suspect 1D DP when you scan a sequence, must choose per position, and the best answer at i depends on a bounded set of earlier answers; the question asks for a max, min, count, or yes/no, and plain recursion shows the same arguments repeating. Siblings: greedy (try a 3-element counterexample first), 2D DP (the state needs two indices or an extra parameter such as remaining capacity), backtracking (when you must list solutions rather than count them), and binary search on the answer. Follow-ups: Climbing Stairs, House Robber II, Coin Change, Longest Increasing Subsequence, Decode Ways, Word Break, Maximum Subarray, Partition Equal Subset Sum.

A DP table has one cell per state and each cell costs O(1) to fill from earlier cells, so a grid DP is O(m * n) time. The fill order must respect dependencies; if the dependencies form a cycle (for instance when moves can go up and left too), DP does not apply and you need graph search.

Be exact about what an index means. In grid problems, dp[r][c] concerns cell (r, c) and the table is m by n. In string problems such as edit distance and LCS, dp[i][j] concerns prefixes of lengths i and j, so the table is (m + 1) by (n + 1), with row 0 and column 0 for the empty prefix. Mixing the two is a classic off-by-one. Typical states: positions in two sequences, or (item index, remaining capacity) for knapsack.

There is a closed form: every path has (m - 1) + (n - 1) = 8 moves, and choosing which 2 are downward gives C(8, 2) = 28, matching the table. The DP extends to obstacles; the closed form is a check. For 100 by 100 the answer is C(198, 99), around 2.3 x 10^58, which overflows 64 bits (LeetCode guarantees the result fits in 2 x 10^9).

Compute binomials iteratively as res = res * (N - k + i) // i, which stays an integer at every step. A 1 by n or m by 1 grid has exactly one path. Variants: Unique Paths II (obstacles), Minimum Path Sum (take min of the two predecessors; the border cannot be filled with 1s but with running sums), Triangle, and Dungeon Game (fill backward from the goal).

Correctness: the last move into (r, c) is either downward from (r-1, c) or rightward from (r, c-1). These cases are exhaustive and disjoint, so the counts add. The border cells have exactly one predecessor, which is why they are all 1s when there are no obstacles. A uniform trick: pad the table with an extra row and column of zeros and seed a single 1 next to the start, so one formula covers every cell.

A Python-specific hazard: dp[r-1][c] with r = 0 does not fail, it wraps to the last row and silently corrupts the answer; handle the borders explicitly. For Minimum Path Sum the base cases are cumulative sums along the first row and column, not ones. If the problem allows moving in four directions, states depend on each other cyclically, and DP no longer applies.

The table is Pascal's triangle rotated: dp[r][c] = C(r + c, r). Row 2 reads C(2,2) = 1, C(3,2) = 3, C(4,2) = 6, C(5,2) = 10, C(6,2) = 15, C(7,2) = 21, C(8,2) = 28, and row 1 reads 1, 2, ..., 7 as C(c+1, 1) shows.

Symmetry: a 3 by 7 grid and a 7 by 3 grid have the same answer, so you can iterate over the smaller dimension to shrink memory to O(min(m, n)). When debugging a DP, compute two or three cells by hand and compare with the program. Printing the table on a small case is the fastest way to find an initialization bug. Fill order is row by row, left to right, so both neighbors are final when a cell is computed.

The code is correct: O(m * n) time and space. The initialization loops can be replaced by dp = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]. Edge cases: when m = 1 or n = 1 the nested loop does not run and dp[m-1][n-1] is 1, as it should be.

The most common Python bug in grid DP is dp = [[0] * n] * m. That creates m references to one list, so writing dp[1][1] changes every row. Always build rows with a comprehension. In C++, vector<vector<int>> dp(m, vector<int>(n, 1)) is safe. Overflow: for large grids the answer exceeds 32 bits, so use long long, though LeetCode keeps the answer within 2 x 10^9. Returning dp[m-1][n-1] rather than dp[n-1][m-1] is another easy slip when m and n differ.

Edit distance: base cases dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j (delete or insert everything). The three options in the else branch correspond to delete from s (dp[i-1][j]), insert into s (dp[i][j-1]), and replace (dp[i-1][j-1]), plus 1. When characters match, taking the diagonal for free is always optimal. Time O(m * n). LCS has zero base cases and the same shape; to print the subsequence itself you walk backward through the full table.

Obstacles: you cannot just fill the first row and column with 1s. Once an obstacle appears, every later cell in that row or column is unreachable and gets 0; if the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Related: Longest Palindromic Subsequence equals LCS of s and its reverse; Distinct Subsequences; Interleaving String; Regular Expression Matching; Coin Change II.

In the compressed update dp[c] += dp[c-1], dp[c] on the right still holds the value from the row above, and dp[c-1] was already updated for the current row (the cell to the left), so scanning left to right is exactly right. Start the single row as all 1s, then process rows 1 through m-1. Space becomes O(n); choose n as the smaller dimension.

When the recurrence also needs the diagonal (edit distance, LCS), save the old dp[j-1] in a temporary variable before overwriting it. Direction is tied to dependencies: in the 0/1 knapsack 1D version you must iterate capacity from high to low so an item is not reused, while unbounded knapsack iterates low to high on purpose. The price: you can no longer reconstruct the path, unless you store decisions or use Hirschberg's method.

Dimension mix-ups: dp[m][n] means m rows and n columns; string DP needs the extra row and column. Initialization: first row and column seed everything, so wrong values spread; for minimum problems use a large sentinel, but not INT_MAX, since adding 1 to it overflows in C++ (use something like 10^9). Iteration direction: every cell must be computed after the cells it reads; reversed loops give silently wrong tables.

Other traps: aliasing rows with [[0]*n]*m, and off-by-one when strings are 0-indexed but dp is length-indexed (compare s[i-1] with t[j-1]). Test 1 by 1 and 1 by n grids, and empty strings: edit distance between '' and 'abc' must be 3. Memoized recursion is a fine alternative, but its depth is about m + n, which is safe unless the grid is huge.
leetcode-dp-02.further: Move from 1D to 2D DP when one parameter is not enough: two sequences being compared (edit distance, LCS), a grid with right/down moves, knapsack-style (item index plus capacity), or interval problems where dp[i][j] covers the substring from i to j. Siblings: 1D DP (a single index), memoized DFS (the same recurrence written top-down), BFS or Dijkstra (grids where you may move in all four directions), backtracking (list the actual solutions), and greedy. If the moves only go forward and you need a count or optimum, think DP. Follow-ups: Minimum Path Sum, Unique Paths II, LCS, Edit Distance, Coin Change II, Target Sum, 0/1 Knapsack, Interleaving String, Maximal Square.

The two properties are the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution contains the greedy first choice) and optimal substructure (what remains after that choice is a smaller instance of the same problem). The exchange argument proves the first: take an optimal solution that differs from greedy, swap in the greedy choice, show it is no worse, and repeat. Stay-ahead proves it by induction: after every step greedy is at least as good as any other strategy, by a stated measure.

Greedy is not universal. Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses two. It does work for US coins. Typical cost is a sort plus one pass, O(n log n). If you cannot prove it, hunt for small counterexamples, or use DP.

For [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] the answer is true; one route is 0 to 1 (jump 1), then 1 to 4 (jump 3). A brute-force search over jump choices is exponential, and a reachability DP is O(n^2). The greedy works because of a key lemma: the set of reachable indices is always a contiguous prefix [0, farthest]. If you can reach j by jumping from i, you can also reach every index between i and j with a shorter jump, so no gaps appear.

Failure example: [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]. The frontier stalls at 3, then i = 4 exceeds it, so the answer is false. A single element is trivially true (you are already at the last index). A 0 is only fatal when it sits at the frontier. Values are nonnegative by definition.

Invariant: before processing index i, every index in [0, farthest] is reachable, and farthest is the maximum of j + nums[j] over all reachable j already scanned. Induction gives it. The failure test is justified: if i > farthest, no reachable index can jump to i or past it, so the end is unreachable. Add an early return as soon as farthest >= n - 1.

Jump Game II (minimum number of jumps) uses the same sweep: keep currentEnd and farthest; whenever i reaches currentEnd, increment the jump count and set currentEnd = farthest. It is a BFS in disguise, where each level is the range of indices reachable with j jumps. O(n) time, O(1) space. Take care not to include i + nums[i] from an unreachable i, which is why the stuck check comes before the update.

Order matters: check i > farthest before updating farthest. For [0, 5, 0, 0], if you updated first, index 1 (unreachable, because nums[0] = 0) would push farthest to 6 and wrongly return true; the check in the right order returns false at i = 1. Time O(n), space O(1).

An equivalent backward formulation: set goal = n - 1, then for i from n-2 down to 0, if i + nums[i] >= goal, set goal = i; the answer is goal == 0. It tracks the leftmost index that can reach the end. Both are the same idea from opposite directions. Overflow is not a concern for typical bounds, but with huge values use 64-bit sums for i + nums[i]. Python's enumerate keeps the loop tidy.

Interval scheduling: sort by finish time and take each interval starting at or after the last chosen finish (use > if touching intervals conflict). Sorting by start fails: for [1,10], [2,3], [4,5], start-order picks [1,10] alone while the optimum is two intervals. Non-overlapping Intervals asks for minimum removals, n minus the maximum kept; Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons is the same sweep.

Gas Station: if total gas is less than total cost, no start exists. Otherwise, scan once, and whenever the tank goes negative at i, restart from i + 1. This is valid because any start between the old start and i would have had a nonnegative tank on the way and so would fail at or before i as well. The total-surplus check guarantees the final candidate completes the loop.

Exchange argument for interval scheduling: let g be the interval with the earliest finish time, and let o1 be the first interval of some optimal solution. Since g finishes no later than o1, replacing o1 with g keeps everything non-overlapping and the size unchanged, so an optimal solution containing g exists. Recurse on the intervals that start after g ends. That is the full proof.

Stay-ahead for Jump Game: after scanning i indices, the greedy frontier is at least as far as the frontier of any other strategy. In an interview, give a two or three sentence version of such an argument, enough to answer 'why can't another choice do better?'. Contrast with DP, which considers every choice; greedy considers one, which is faster but must be justified. Search for counterexamples on arrays of size 3 or 4 first.

Greedy without proof is the main risk: a plausible rule that fails hidden tests. 'Largest first' or 'smallest first' are the usual wrong guesses, as in coin change with [1, 3, 4]. The right question is not 'which choice looks best now?' but 'which choice leaves the most freedom for what follows?', which is why interval scheduling sorts by finish time.

Watch the sort key and tie-breaking, and decide whether touching endpoints conflict. Off-by-one in reachability (i > farthest versus i >= farthest) flips answers. Remember the last-index cases: n = 1 is true. A practical safeguard is stress testing: generate small random inputs, compare your greedy with a brute force or DP, and look for the first disagreement. Some problems that feel greedy need extra structure, such as Remove K Digits with a monotonic stack.
leetcode-greedy-01.further: Consider greedy when a problem asks for a minimum or maximum count of something and a simple rule ('earliest finish', 'smallest first', 'farthest reach') seems to keep every option open: scheduling, covering, reachability, and resource-allocation questions. Siblings: DP (considers all choices; the fallback when a counterexample appears), BFS (fewest steps; Jump Game II is BFS in disguise), heap-assisted greedy (pick the best available at each step, as in Task Scheduler and Meeting Rooms II), and interval sweeps. First try to break your rule on four elements; if it breaks, move to DP. Follow-ups: Jump Game II, Gas Station, Non-overlapping Intervals, Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons, Partition Labels, Task Scheduler, Candy.

Two closed intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap exactly when a <= d and c <= b, regardless of which comes first; for half-open intervals the test is a < d and c < b. A degenerate closed interval [x, x] is a single point and is valid; a half-open [x, x) is empty. Confirm with the interviewer or the examples which convention applies.

Also ask: may the input be unsorted? Can intervals be identical or nested? Are coordinates negative or huge? Is start <= end guaranteed? For lengths of closed integer intervals use end - start + 1, and watch for overflow near 32-bit limits. Everything below assumes a list of [start, end] pairs and the closed convention used by Merge Intervals.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates; the sweep after it is O(n); the output takes O(n) space. The naive alternative compares all pairs, O(n^2), and still needs repeated passes because merging two intervals can create overlap with a third, so chains require transitive closure.

Edge cases: empty input returns []; a single interval returns itself; duplicates collapse; and containment must work: [1, 10] and [2, 3] merge into [1, 10], not [1, 3]. That is why the merged end is a max, never a plain assignment. The result is sorted and disjoint, with a strict gap between neighbors: each next start is greater than the previous end. Unsorted input such as [[8,10],[1,3],[2,6]] must be sorted first; Python's default list ordering sorts by start, then end, which is fine here.

Proof sketch of the sweep. After sorting by start, every unprocessed interval starts at or after the current one. If curr.start > last.end, no later interval can reach back to last either, since later starts are even larger, so last is final. If curr.start <= last.end, then curr starts inside last (its start is at least last.start by sorting), so they overlap and the union is a single interval from last.start to max of the ends. Ties on start do not matter.

The crucial detail is comparing against last.end, the merged end, not the previous input interval's end. With [1,10], [2,3], [4,5], the third interval must be tested against 10 (it merges), not against 3 (it would wrongly stay separate).

Merging uses the max of the ends because the current interval may be contained in the last one. A subtle trap: if last = intervals[0] aliases the caller's list, the update last.end = max(...) mutates the input, so copy it (as the pseudocode does) or build the answer directly: for each [s, e] in sorted order, if res is non-empty and s <= res[-1][1], set res[-1][1] = max(res[-1][1], e); else append [s, e]. That version also handles the empty list with no special case and has no final flush step.

Both versions are O(n log n) time and O(n) output space. Each interval is touched once after sorting. Remember that adjacent output intervals never touch: if they did, they would have merged.

Common slips: forgetting the final res.append(last) loses the last group; forgetting the empty-input guard crashes on intervals[0]; sorting by end or not sorting at all; using < instead of <= for closed intervals, which leaves [1,4] and [4,5] unmerged. Test cases worth running: [[1,4],[4,5]] gives [[1,5]]; [[1,4],[0,4]] gives [[0,4]]; [[1,4],[0,0]] gives [[0,0],[1,4]]; and [[2,3],[4,5],[6,7],[8,9],[1,10]] gives [[1,10]].

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) for the output, plus whatever the sort uses (Python's Timsort needs up to O(n) auxiliary; an in-place quicksort or heapsort uses less). If the input is already sorted by start, as in Insert Interval, the whole job drops to O(n).

Meeting Rooms I: sort by start and check whether any start is less than the previous end (with half-open meaning). Meeting Rooms II asks for the maximum number of simultaneous intervals: sort starts and ends separately and sweep with two pointers, or use a min-heap of end times; both O(n log n). In the sweep-line view, each interval adds +1 at its start and -1 at its end; at equal times process ends first for half-open intervals.

Insert Interval (sorted, disjoint input) needs no sort: add everything ending before the new start, merge everything that overlaps by taking min of starts and max of ends, then add the rest, in O(n). Interval List Intersections walks two sorted lists with two pointers in O(m + n). Others: Employee Free Time, Car Pooling, My Calendar, and the greedy Non-overlapping Intervals.

Semantics decide the comparison. Closed [1,3] and [3,5] share the point 3, so they merge into [1,5]. Half-open [1,3) and [3,5) do not overlap, so they stay separate; the merge condition becomes curr.start < last.end. Real calendars are usually half-open: a meeting ending at 10 does not conflict with one starting at 10. LeetCode's Merge Intervals treats touching intervals as overlapping, while Meeting Rooms treats them as compatible. Read the examples.

For integers, a closed [a, b] equals the half-open [a, b+1), a handy conversion. Floating-point endpoints make equality tests fragile. Zero-length intervals deserve a test. In Car Pooling, passengers leaving at a stop are removed before those boarding at the same stop, which is the half-open rule in disguise.

Sorting by start is what makes the single sweep valid. The page's sort-by-end order is off: [2,6] ends before [8,10], so this example sorts the same either way. A real failure is [1,10], [2,3], [4,5]: sorted by end it becomes [2,3], [4,5], [1,10], so the sweep finalizes [2,3], then meets [1,10], which overlaps that finalized interval, and the output is wrong. Sorting by end is the right key for a different problem, greedy selection of the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals.

Ties in start do not affect merging. Already-sorted input (Insert Interval) skips the cost. In Java, comparators written as a[0] - b[0] can overflow for extreme values; use Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]). Python's list.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) is stable, which is harmless here. If intervals arrive online with queries in between, a sorted container or balanced tree is better than re-sorting.
leetcode-greedy-02.further: Reach for interval techniques when the data are ranges on a line (times, positions, ids) and you must merge, insert, count overlaps, find gaps, or schedule. Keywords: overlapping, meetings, free time, minimum rooms. Siblings: greedy selection (sort by end), heap (track the earliest ending interval), sweep line or difference array (counts of active intervals), two pointers on sorted lists (intersections), and segment or balanced trees when intervals arrive online. Quick split: merging means sort by start; maximizing kept non-overlapping intervals means sort by end. Follow-ups: Insert Interval, Meeting Rooms I and II, Non-overlapping Intervals, Interval List Intersections, Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons, Employee Free Time, Car Pooling.

Conventions vary, so define a monotonic stack by its pop rule. To keep the stack non-decreasing from bottom to top, pop while top > x before pushing x. Each popped element has just found its next smaller element, which is x; and after popping, the element now on top is x's previous smaller (or equal) element. The opposite rule (pop while top < x) produces a non-increasing stack, the one used for next greater problems.

Small run on [3, 1, 2]: push 3; x = 1 pops 3 (its next smaller is 1), push 1; x = 2 does not pop 1, push 2; the stack is [1, 2], non-decreasing. Whether equality pops (> versus >=) is a design choice that controls whether duplicates count as smaller.

The decreasing stack (pop while top < x) keeps values non-increasing from bottom to top, and each pop resolves a next greater element: the element that pops j is the first later element strictly greater than it. Daily Temperatures uses exactly this rule, so the trace in the next panel is consistent with it. Using top <= x would instead find the next greater-or-equal element.

Elements still on the stack at the end never found an answer, so default their result to 0 or -1. For circular arrays (Next Greater Element II), iterate i from 0 to 2n - 1 and read nums[i % n], pushing indices only during the first pass. Always keep the stack of indices so you can look up values by index and compute distances; the stack's values are then non-increasing by construction.

The answer is [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]. Index 2 (75) waits until 76 at index 6, so 4 days; index 3 (71) is resolved by 72 at index 5, so 2 days. At the end the stack holds indices 6 and 7, whose answers stay 0.

Useful extremes: a strictly decreasing input never pops, so everything is 0 and the stack grows to n; a strictly increasing input pops each previous element immediately, so each answer is 1 except the last; equal temperatures are not warmer, so they stay stacked and resolve only against something strictly warmer. At every moment the stack holds the days still waiting for a warmer day, in order of non-increasing temperature.

Time O(n), space O(n) (up to n when temperatures never rise). Initializing ans with zeros handles the no-answer case for free. A frequent bug is writing T[i] >= T[st.top()], which treats an equal temperature as warmer; another is using if instead of while, which pops only one element per step and misses chained resolutions like index 6 popping two entries (indices 5 and 2).

An alternative with no stack scans right to left and uses the answers already computed to jump ahead: for i, set j = i + 1 and while T[j] <= T[i], jump j += ans[j] (stop if ans[j] is 0). It is also O(n) amortized. A right-to-left stack version pops while top <= x and then reads the top as the answer, then pushes x. Choose whichever direction makes your final bookkeeping simplest.

Next greater for [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]: the first 2 has next strictly greater 4, not the second 2 (equal is not greater). The answer is [4, 2, 4, -1, -1], which fits. Largest rectangle in [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]: use the increasing stack with a sentinel height 0 appended; when index j is popped at position i, width is i - (new top + 1), or i if the stack is empty, and area is height * width. Bars 5 and 6 give 5 * 2 = 10; the 2 at index 4 spans width 4, area 8; the 1 spans all 6, area 6. Best is 10.

Stock span pops while price <= today; the example gives 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 6. Also: Trapping Rain Water, Sum of Subarray Minimums, Remove K Digits.

Amortized analysis: each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so across the entire loop there are at most 2n stack operations. The inner while loop may run many times in a single iteration, but those pops are paid for by earlier pushes; the total work cannot exceed n pops. Hence O(n), not O(n^2), despite the nesting.

The contrast is the naive method that scans forward from each index to find its answer, which costs O(n) per index and O(n^2) overall on inputs like a long decreasing sequence followed by a large value. The accounting idea is the same one used in dynamic array growth and in sliding pointers: potential equals current stack size, each push adds 1 unit, each pop spends 1. Space is O(n) in the worst case, when nothing ever pops.

Store indices (or value-and-index pairs), never bare values. You need positions for distances and widths, and with duplicates a bare value cannot tell you which occurrence was popped.

For problems needing both a left and right boundary (histograms, Sum of Subarray Minimums), one pass gives both: the element that pops j is its right boundary, and the new top is its left boundary. With equal elements, use strict comparison on one side and non-strict on the other, or equal subarrays are counted twice. Remember to flush the stack at the end, typically with a sentinel (a height-0 bar) or a second loop. Take the left boundary as -1 when the stack is empty.

Pop rules, restated. Pop while top < x leaves a non-increasing stack and finds the next greater. Pop while top > x leaves a non-decreasing stack and finds the next smaller. Mnemonic: pop the entries that the new element beats in the direction you are searching. Non-strict versions (<= and >=) change whether ties count as answers; pick one deliberately.

To find a previous greater or smaller element, the one left on top after the popping is done is the answer for x, before you push x. For windows rather than whole arrays, switch to a monotonic deque: also pop from the front when an index leaves the window, which solves Sliding Window Maximum in O(n). Every variant has the same skeleton: maintain order by popping, record answers at pop time (right side) or push time (left side).
leetcode-stacks-02.further: Think monotonic stack when the question is about the nearest element to the left or right that is greater or smaller, or about spans, bars, and areas that extend until something blocks them: next greater element, daily temperatures, histogram rectangles, stock spans, and 'remove digits to make the smallest number'. Siblings: a plain stack (matching and nesting), monotonic deque (extreme within a sliding window), heap (extreme over everything seen, not the nearest), and prefix or suffix maximum arrays (an alternative for Trapping Rain Water). Follow-ups: Next Greater Element I and II, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Maximal Rectangle, Trapping Rain Water, Online Stock Span, Sum of Subarray Minimums, Remove K Digits, 132 Pattern.

P has n + 1 entries, with P[0] = 0 representing the empty prefix. Building it is O(n) time and O(n) space; afterwards every range sum is O(1), so q queries cost O(n + q) instead of O(n * q). Check: for A = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], the running totals 3, 4, 8, 9, 14 give P = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14].

The trick works for any operation with an inverse: addition (subtraction undoes it), XOR (it undoes itself: P[r+1] ^ P[l]), and counts of anything. It does not work for min or max, which have no inverse; use a sparse table or segment tree. Sums can exceed 32 bits (n * max), so use 64-bit integers. The array must be static; with updates use a Fenwick or segment tree, O(log n) each.

Range sum over the inclusive range [l, r] is P[r+1] - P[l]. Check the edges: l = r gives P[l+1] - P[l] = A[l]; the whole array gives P[n] - P[0]; an empty range (l = r + 1) gives 0. For the example, A[1..3] = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, which matches 9 - 3.

The leading zero is not decoration. If you define P[i] as the sum through index i, the formula becomes P[r] - P[l-1], and l = 0 needs a special case. Padding with P[0] = 0 removes that branch and most off-by-one errors.

The inverse operation is the difference array: add v to a range in O(1) by D[l] += v and D[r+1] -= v, then recover final values with a prefix sum. It powers Corporate Flight Bookings and Car Pooling.

Why not a sliding window: nums may contain negatives and zeros, so the window sum is not monotone, and shrinking or growing it tells you nothing. Prefix sums work for any integers. A subarray A[i..j] has sum P[j+1] - P[i]; it equals k exactly when P[i] = P[j+1] - k. So the problem becomes counting earlier prefix values that equal the needed one. Brute force is O(n^2); the hash map brings it to O(n).

Counts, not a set, are required: for [0, 0, 0] and k = 0 every one of the 6 subarrays qualifies, and the prefix values are 0, 0, 0, 0 with C(4,2) = 6 matching pairs. The answer can reach n(n+1)/2, so use 64-bit. Related: Contiguous Array (map 0 to -1), Subarray Sums Divisible by K (track prefix mod k).

Trace for [1, 1, 1], k = 2. Start freq = {0: 1}. x = 1: sum = 1, need -1, no match, record 1. x = 1: sum = 2, need 0, freq[0] = 1 so count = 1 (subarray [0..1]), record 2. x = 1: sum = 3, need 1, freq[1] = 1 so count = 2 (subarray [1..2]). The table in the text is the map after the loop ends.

Correctness: each valid subarray ending at j corresponds to exactly one earlier prefix equal to S - k, and the map holds counts of earlier prefixes only because each prefix is recorded after its own lookup. Time O(n) expected; space up to n + 1 distinct sums. The map must start with the empty prefix 0, because a subarray beginning at index 0 matches against it.

Order of operations matters when k = 0. If you record the current sum before looking up sum - k, then with k = 0 the lookup finds the prefix you just inserted, counting an empty subarray every time. On [1, 1, 1] with k = 0 that gives 3 instead of the correct 0. Lookup first, then record.

Smaller points: reading freq[sum - k] on a defaultdict inserts the key; use freq.get(sum - k, 0) to keep the map tidy. Naming a variable sum shadows Python's built-in. In C++ or Java, use long long for the running sum, and compute sum - k in 64 bits. If every number is nonnegative and the question is only about 'at least' or 'at most' sums, a sliding window achieves the same with O(1) space. The map approach is the general tool.

For a matrix, build P as (n+1) by (m+1) with P[i+1][j+1] = A[i][j] + P[i][j+1] + P[i+1][j] - P[i][j]: the two strips overlap in P[i][j], which is subtracted once. The query then follows inclusion-exclusion: take the big rectangle, subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, add back the corner removed twice. Build is O(n * m), each query O(1), and the zero padding row and column avoid edge checks.

Direct applications: Range Sum Query 2D Immutable. Harder: Count Submatrices With Sum Target, where you fix two rows, collapse the columns into a 1D array, and reuse the subarray-sum hash map in O(n^2 * m). Maximum sum rectangle no larger than K combines this with a sorted set. In d dimensions, inclusion-exclusion has 2^d terms.

Initialize freq[0] = 1; without it, subarrays starting at index 0 are missed. Negative numbers: prefix sums plus hashing handle them; sliding windows do not. Index conventions: keep P[i] meaning 'sum of the first i elements' everywhere, and write the query as P[r+1] - P[l] each time.

In 'longest subarray' variants (Contiguous Array, Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k), store only the first index at which each prefix value appears and do not overwrite it; the longest subarray uses the earliest matching prefix. With remainders, negative modulo differs by language: in C++ and Java, use ((s % k) + k) % k; Python's % already returns a nonnegative value.

Updates invalidate a prefix array, so rebuild at O(n) or switch to a Fenwick tree. Using the input array as the prefix array saves memory but destroys the original.
leetcode-arrays-04.further: Use prefix sums when you face many range-sum queries on fixed data, or when you must count or find subarrays whose sum, XOR, or remainder meets a condition, especially with negative numbers. Siblings: sliding window (nonnegative values, monotone constraints, O(1) space), Kadane's algorithm (maximum subarray sum with no target), Fenwick tree or segment tree (range queries with updates), difference arrays (range updates), and hashing (here applied to prefix values). Quick split: negatives or exact-sum counting call for prefix plus hash; positives with longest or shortest windows call for a sliding window. Follow-ups: Range Sum Query, Contiguous Array, Subarray Sums Divisible by K, Product of Array Except Self, Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k, Corporate Flight Bookings.

Place values: 101101 is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. A w-bit unsigned integer holds 0 to 2^w - 1. Signed integers use two's complement: the top bit carries weight -2^(w-1), so a 32-bit int spans -2^31 to 2^31 - 1, and -x equals ~x + 1; -1 is all ones. The number of bits needed for n is floor(log2 n) + 1, and a power of two has exactly one set bit.

Python integers have unlimited width, with negatives behaving as if sign-extended forever; to emulate 32-bit behavior, mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF and convert back if the top bit is set. Counting set bits (popcount) is easy with Kernighan's loop: while n: n &= n - 1; count += 1, which runs once per set bit. Related warm-ups: Number of 1 Bits, Reverse Bits, Hamming Distance.

For A = 10110 (22), ~A is 01001 only if you keep five bits. In 8 bits the leading zeros flip too, giving 11101001. Left shift 10110 << 2 is 1011000 (88), which widens the value; in a 5-bit register the top bits fall off and you get 11000. Right shift 10110 >> 2 is 101, i.e. 00101 in five bits (22 // 4 = 5).

AND, OR, XOR rows check out: 22 & 13 = 4, 22 | 13 = 31, 22 ^ 13 = 27. Shifts: x << k is x * 2^k when nothing overflows; x >> k is floor(x / 2^k), so an arithmetic shift of a negative number rounds toward negative infinity: -5 >> 1 is -3, whereas C's -5 / 2 gives -2.

Why it works: XOR is commutative and associative, x ^ x = 0, and x ^ 0 = x. The XOR of the whole array rearranges so each pair meets and cancels, leaving only the unpaired element. Time O(n), space O(1), versus O(n) space for a hash set. It requires every other value to appear exactly twice (or an even number of times); negatives work unchanged.

Variants show the idea's reach. Single Number II (others appear three times): count each bit position modulo 3. Single Number III (two unpaired values a and b): XOR everything to get a ^ b, isolate one set bit with d = x & -x, split the numbers into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group. Missing Number: XOR the indices 0 to n with all values.

Beyond the four basics: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit (in two's complement, -x flips everything above that bit), and x & (x - 1) clears it. Use (x >> i) & 1 when you need a clean 0 or 1, since x & mask returns a nonzero value, not necessarily 1.

Width traps: in C or C++, 1 << 31 on a 32-bit int overflows into the sign bit (undefined behavior before C++20), so use 1LL << i or 1ULL << i for large i. In Java, shifting an int by 32 or more uses the count modulo 32, so 1 << 32 is 1; use 1L << i for long values. Python has no such limits, and x & ~mask works because ~mask is simply a negative number with infinite leading ones.

Subset enumeration: for mask in range(1 << n), the set bits select the chosen elements; O(n * 2^n), practical up to n of about 20. Submask enumeration, for sub = mask; sub > 0; sub = (sub - 1) & mask, visits every nonempty submask; summed over all masks, the cost is 3^n. Bitmask DP stores state as a mask: Traveling Salesman runs in O(2^n * n^2), Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets in O(2^n * n).

Power of two: x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0; the x > 0 check matters, since 0 would pass otherwise. Counting bits via DP: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). A 26-bit mask can record which letters a word contains. Avoid the XOR swap trick on aliased variables: x ^= x yields zero.

Precedence: in C, C++, and Java, == binds tighter than &, |, and ^. So x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0): C and C++ compile it and give the wrong answer; Java rejects it as a type error. Python is the opposite, since bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so x & 1 == 0 works there; parenthesize anyway for readability.

Signed shifts: right-shifting a negative signed integer was implementation-defined in C and C++ (arithmetic in practice, defined as arithmetic from C++20), while Java offers >> (arithmetic) and >>> (logical). The example is right: -4 as 8 bits is 11111100; arithmetic >> 1 gives 11111110 (-2); a logical shift gives 01111110 (126). Shifting by the full width or more is undefined in C and C++. Prefer unsigned types for bit tricks.
leetcode-bits-01.further: Consider bit manipulation when pairs cancel or parity matters (XOR), when you must enumerate subsets of about 20 or fewer items (bitmasks), when a handful of boolean flags can be packed into one integer for DP states or visited sets, or when the problem is about binary representation: counting bits, powers of two, reversing, adding without a plus. Siblings: hashing and counting (general frequencies at O(n) space), math formulas (such as the sum trick for Missing Number), sorting then scanning, and backtracking (enumerate with undo when state is large). Follow-ups: Number of 1 Bits, Counting Bits, Reverse Bits, Missing Number, Single Number II and III, Sum of Two Integers, Maximum XOR of Two Numbers.
